Our results also highlight the benefits of incorporating first-order optimization techniques. Point cloud analysis has become a crucial component in numerous applications, such as 3D object recognition, autonomous driving, and 3D scene understanding. However, existing deep learning methods for point clouds often struggle with limited receptive fields and inefficient processing. To address these issues, we introduce the Multi Point-Voxel Convolution (MPVConv) module, which leverages the concept of point-voxel convolution. By combining the strengths of both point and voxel convolutions, MPVConv enables the simultaneous consideration of local point features and global voxel information. This innovative approach is achieved through the utilization of two types of voxelization methods, which allow for the efficient aggregation of features from both local and global perspectives. Our proposed method, MPVConv, has been successfully integrated into a novel network, MPVConvNet, which demonstrates exceptional performance on various 3D object recognition benchmarks. Furthermore, we have developed a new dataset, ScanObjectNN, which addresses the limitations of existing datasets by providing a more comprehensive and challenging set of 3D object recognition tasks. The ScanObjectNN dataset features a diverse set of objects, including complex and occluded parts, which are essential for the development of robust 3D object recognition models. Our experiments demonstrate that MPVConvNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on ScanObjectNN, outperforming other methods by a significant margin. These findings are supported by numerical simulations that validate our theoretical results. Lastly, we discuss potential avenues for further research and pose several open questions in this area. By applying a control signal to the actuator, the resonator's frequency can be adjusted in real-time, effectively compensating for frequency shifts caused by microphonics. This method has been successfully demonstrated using a 1.5 GHz resonator, showcasing its ability to counteract detuning and maintain a stable resonant frequency. Furthermore, the study explores the potential of this technique to enhance the performance of quantum devices, such as superconducting qubits, by mitigating the effects of microphonics-induced detuning. Face recognition technology has become ubiquitous in our daily lives, but it's also vulnerable to sophisticated cyber threats. This approach involves identifying and removing malicious samples from the training data, significantly improving model performance. Our experiments demonstrate that this method can effectively eliminate backdoor attacks and enhance model security without sacrificing performance. This research has significant implications for the development of trustworthy face recognition systems, which are essential for their widespread adoption. blockchain architectures, instead employing a directed acyclic graph to validate
transactions. By eliminating the need for a central authority, Tangle 2.0 enables
efficient transaction confirmation through a decentralized process. In this context,
we introduce a new consensus algorithm, the Heaviest DAG, which is designed to
operate within Tangle 2.0. By leveraging this algorithm, Tangle 2.0 can effectively
achieve consensus without reliance on a centralized entity. Furthermore, we
examine the Heaviest DAG's resilience to various attacks, including double-spending,
fork attacks, and 51% attacks, and demonstrate its ability to operate in a
distributed setting. By providing a comprehensive analysis of Tangle 2.0's
consensus algorithm, we aim to facilitate a deeper understanding of its
operational mechanics. In addition, we provide a detailed comparison of the
Heaviest DAG with existing consensus algorithms, highlighting its unique
characteristics and distinct advantages. By shedding light on the intricacies of
Tangle 2.0's consensus algorithm, we aim to contribute to the development of
efficient and secure blockchain solutions. Finally, we outline potential avenues
for future research, which may involve the application of the Heaviest DAG to
other distributed systems and the exploration of alternative consensus algorithms
for Tangle 2.0. By providing a comprehensive analysis of the Heaviest DAG, we
aim to provide a solid foundation for the development of blockchain solutions. The

The task of identifying films from their trailers or clips is known as film recognition. This task is particularly challenging due to the similarities in visual and linguistic content found in trailers and clips of the same film. In this study, we investigate the effectiveness of using a classifier to tackle film recognition. We propose a novel approach that involves fine-tuning a pre-trained vision-language model on a large-scale image-text dataset and then using it to generate a text representation of the film clip. This representation is then used to train a classifier to distinguish between different films. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach achieves state-of-the-art results on the UCF101-Film and UCF101-Text datasets. Furthermore, we show that our method can be improved by incorporating additional information, such as film titles and genres, to provide more context for the classifier. We investigate the suitability of factor models for mortality prediction, focusing on the time-constant vs. time-variant factor loading approach. To this end, we develop a new factor model that incorporates both static and dynamic loading components, allowing us to analyze the time-constant and time-variant factor models within a unified framework. Our analysis reveals that the time-variant factor model generally outperforms its time-constant counterpart, with the latter's performance being particularly poor for older ages. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the time-variant factor model can be efficiently estimated using a computationally simple method. Our results are substantiated through a comprehensive Monte Carlo study and an empirical analysis of the French male population. The findings suggest that the time-variant factor model is a more effective tool for mortality prediction, particularly for older ages. Moreover, we provide a practical implementation of the time-variant factor model in R, making it accessible to researchers and practitioners. Our results also highlight the potential benefits of multi-task learning in sequence forecasting tasks. Furthermore, we release our TATAM dataset and implementation to facilitate future research in this area. This paper is the second installment in a two-part series focusing on the transmitter design for the emerging orthogonal time-frequency domain modulation (OTFDm) technique. OTFDm is a multi-carrier modulation that diverges from the conventional orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) approach by dispensing with the fast Fourier transform (FFT) structure. Instead, OTFDm employs a unique time-domain processing method, where the real and imaginary parts of the modulated symbols are transmitted in separate time slots. This innovative approach enables OTFDm to offer enhanced spectral efficiency, improved resistance to phase noise, and reduced peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) compared to OFDM. The first part of the paper introduced OTFDm's fundamental principles and potential benefits, while this second installment delves into the design of transmitter structures for OTFDm. The paper presents a range of transmitter designs, categorized into three distinct classes, and evaluates their performance in terms of spectral efficiency, PAPR, and implementation complexity. The results demonstrate that OTFDm can achieve a 33% increase in spectral efficiency and a 10-dB reduction in PAPR compared to OFDM, while maintaining a comparable implementation complexity. The paper also explores the potential for OTFDm to be integrated with existing transceiver architectures, such as those used in 5G and future wireless communication systems.
